# PHP How to Import All Classes from Another Namespace

You cannot import an entire namespace into your current scope using a single statement like `use \foo;`. This is a common misconception when migrating legacy codebases to modern namespaces. The language specification treats the `use` keyword as a directive for specific class imports, not as a mechanism for importing whole directories or namespace containers.

Attempting to write `use \foo;` in the global namespace will result in a syntax error or simply fail to register the classes within that scope. When you declare a namespace, PHP expects explicit bindings for every class you intend to reference. If you try to access `\foo\bar` without importing it, or if you attempt to use `use \foo;` expecting it to magically populate your global scope with `bar`, the parser will reject it because no specific class named `foo` exists at that level to be imported as an alias.

### The Grouped Use Declaration

While you cannot import a namespace wholesale, PHP 7 introduced grouped declarations to streamline the process when dealing with many classes within a single external namespace. Before version 7, developers were forced to write verbose lines for every class they needed:

```php
use Some\Namespace\ClassA;
use Some\Namespace\ClassB;
use Some\Namespace\ClassC as C;
```

This verbosity increases the risk of typos and makes refactoring tedious if the external namespace structure changes. PHP 7 allows you to group these declarations into a single statement using curly braces:

```php
use Some\Namespace\{ClassA, ClassB, ClassC as C};
```

Although this syntax does not import the entire namespace hierarchy, it significantly reduces boilerplate code when referencing multiple classes from one source. This is particularly useful if you are creating a facade or a service layer that aggregates functionality from a third-party library. You can group all necessary imports in one line without sacrificing the explicitness of which specific classes are being brought into scope.

### Why Not Import Everything?

The limitation exists for a reason: maintainability and clarity. Explicit imports make it immediately obvious to any developer reading your code exactly which external dependencies are active. If you could import an entire namespace with `use \Vendor\Package;`, the resulting class map would become ambiguous. You wouldn't know if `Vendor\Package\Controller` is available or if the author intended to use `Vendor\Package\Model`.

Furthermore, importing every single class in a large namespace can lead to unused code being included in your autoloader's resolution path. Modern PHP frameworks and autoloinders (like those used with Composer) rely on specific class paths. By explicitly listing only what you need via grouped declarations, you ensure that your application loads only the required components. This keeps memory usage low and prevents potential naming collisions where a generic `use \Vendor;` might accidentally shadow an internal class of the same name.

### Practical Migration Strategy

When refactoring an existing project to implement namespaces, do not attempt to find a shortcut to import everything at once. Instead, audit your codebase to identify which external classes are actually referenced. Once identified, apply grouped `use` statements for those specific classes.

If you are working with a library where every class in the root namespace is relevant, you can still iterate through them or use tools to generate the grouped `use` statement automatically. However, there is no native PHP construct that acts as a wildcard import for an entire namespace scope. The trade-off between verbosity and ambiguity favors the explicit approach, even with grouping. Stick to specific imports to ensure your code remains readable and predictable.
